transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, doctor, it's... it's mostly about what's been happening over at the church. I've been going to the same church for, oh, it must be near forty years now, ever since we moved to this side of town, and I always help out. I always do. But lately, I... well, I came because I just keep doing these odd things, and it's getting folks to staring at me. 

We have these potlucks down in the fellowship hall, you see, usually on the first Sunday, and I always volunteer to help serve because I like to make sure everybody gets a good portion. But just the other week, I was standing right there by the potluck table, and I picked up the serving spoon—the big metal one for the potato salad—and I just held it up in the air. I just stood there holding it up and I didn't move. I don't even know how long I was stuck like that, just frozen with my arm up in the air, not scooping, not serving, just holding the spoon while everybody was wondering what on earth I was doing. 

And it wasn't just that one time, either. Another time, they had me on the end of the table with the cutlery and the napkins. We use those thick paper ones, the nice square ones, and I was supposed to be passing them out. But instead of handing them to the folks in line, I just started folding the same stack of napkins over and over. I'd fold them, and press the edges, and just keep messing with that exact same stack, making the creases tighter and tighter. There was a whole line of people waiting on me, just standing there with their plates needing a napkin, and I couldn't seem to stop myself from just folding that same pile over and over again until Sister Martha had to come tap my shoulder and take them from me. It's just so embarrassing, and I don't know why I get stuck doing these strange things, but I figured I better come talk to somebody about it because it's just not like me to hold up the dinner line.
Do you feel upset or bothered by these odd things you've been doing at church?

Well, doctor, I don't know if "upset" is exactly the right word... I'm not sitting at home crying my eyes out over it, if that's what you mean. But bothered? Oh, Lord, yes, I am bothered. It's just... it's the look on everybody's faces, you know? 

Like I was saying, I've been at that church near forty years. I know everybody's children, and their children's children. I watched most of them grow up right there in those pews. And when you're standing there holding a big old metal spoon up to the ceiling like some kind of statue... well, it just makes you feel plain foolish. Sister Martha, bless her heart, she didn't say a mean word to me when she took those napkins out of my hands the other time. She just patted my arm real gentle. But I could see the line of folks behind her stretching all the way back to the double doors of the fellowship hall. 

And Pastor Higgins was in that line, too! He always comes through early because he likes the end piece of the baked ham, always has, ever since he took over the parish. And to think I was holding up the Pastor and everybody else just because my hands wanted to keep pressing those napkin creases tighter and tighter... it just doesn't make a lick of sense to me. 

I don't feel angry or anything, just... confused, I suppose. It bothers me that I can't just serve a plate like a regular person anymore. I mean, what if they don't want me at the serving table next month? I've always been at the serving table. Since 1985, at least. Maybe '84, right around the time they put the new linoleum in the kitchen. If I can't help with the potluck, well, I just don't know what I'd do with myself on a Sunday afternoon. So yes, it does bother me quite a bit to be acting so strange.
Do you feel anxious or nervous before these strange things happen, like holding the spoon or folding the napkins?

Well, no, not really. I don't get a flutter in my chest or anything like that before it happens. It's not like when I have to get up and do the scripture reading on the fifth Sunday—now that makes me nervous, always has. I get right up there to the lectern, the wooden one with the little brass lamp, and my palms get all sweaty just thinking about pronouncing those long names in the Old Testament. But this? No, it's not like that at all. 

I'll just be standing there, plain as day, feeling perfectly fine. Like with the spoon, I was just thinking about how Mrs. Gable always puts too much mayonnaise in her potato salad—she’s been doing it since the nineties, bless her, and it just gets so runny if it sits out too long. I was just thinking about that, and going to scoop a good solid portion from the bottom where it's thicker, and then... it just happens. No warning. No racing heart, no shaking hands, no feeling like something bad is about to happen. 

Same with the napkins. I was just standing there, humming a little bit of 'How Great Thou Art'—the choir had just sung it that morning, and it always gets stuck in my head, especially the second verse—and I just picked up the stack. I wasn't worried about dropping them or anything. I just started folding. It's like my body just decides to do something else entirely, and my mind is just sort of... along for the ride, I guess. So, no, doctor, I wouldn't say I feel anxious before it starts. It just sneaks up on me out of nowhere, right in the middle of a perfectly normal thought about mayonnaise or a hymn.
Have you ever found yourself doing these strange, repetitive things when you're not at church?

Well, now that you mention it... I suppose it's not just at the fellowship hall, though that's where it bothers me the most because of all the folks watching. But yes, it has happened at home, too. Just the other day, I was in my kitchen. It's a nice little kitchen, gets the morning sun right through the window over the sink. I have these yellow curtains up, the ones with the little white daisies I bought at the Sears Roebuck before they closed down the one out by the highway. Anyway, I was standing there at the sink, washing up my breakfast dishes. I always have a bowl of oatmeal, you know, with a little brown sugar and a splash of milk, just like my mother used to make. 

I had the dishcloth in my hand—the blue one with the waffle weave, not the smooth ones, I don't like how those smooth ones don't scrub right—and I was just wiping the rim of my oatmeal bowl. And then... I just kept wiping. Over and over, round and round that same little rim. I wasn't even looking at the bowl anymore, I was looking out the window at Mrs. Higgins' cat—the orange tabby, he always comes digging in my flowerbeds—but my hand just kept going in circles. Round and round and round. I must have stood there for ten minutes just wiping a perfectly clean bowl until my elbow started to ache. 

And another time, I was out on the front porch. I like to sweep the porch on Tuesdays, it's just a habit I got into back when the street sweeper used to come by on Mondays and kick up all the dust. I had my good broom, the one with the natural bristles, and I went to sweep a little pile of oak leaves off the top step. But instead of sweeping them off, I just stood there with the broom lifted up, just holding it out over the step. Like I was stuck. Just like with that big metal serving spoon at the church potluck, you know? I just froze there, holding the broom up in the air, while the wind just blew the leaves away on its own. So yes, doctor, it does happen when I'm just by myself, doing my regular chores. It's just so peculiar, isn't it? Just standing there holding a spoon or a broom up to the sky for no good reason at all.
Do you find that these episodes affect your daily life or relationships outside of church?

Well, to be honest with you, it really has put a damper on my day-to-day routine, especially with my friends. You see, I've always been one to keep busy. Idle hands are the devil's workshop, my mother used to say. She pulled me out of school in the eighth grade to help out at home, so keeping busy and working hard is really all I know how to do. 

But lately... well, I've actually had to step back from the choir and a lot of my other church volunteering. I sing alto, you know. Have since I was just a young girl, back when we didn't even have the big organ in the sanctuary, just an old upright piano. But I started getting all the plans mixed up. I'd tell folks the wrong dates for the winter clothing drive, or I'd show up for choir practice on a Tuesday when it's always been on Wednesday, ever since Mr. Henderson took over as director. I'd get the phone tree schedule completely backwards. It just got to be too confusing. 

And the other ladies... well, I could tell they were getting mighty uncomfortable around me. They wouldn't say a mean word to my face, of course, because they're good Christian women, but I'd see them exchanging looks when I'd get confused about what we were doing. And then they'd have to go behind my back and redo the schedules or reorganize the donation boxes I was supposed to handle, just to fix my messes. It just breaks my heart, it really does, having to step back from all that. It's my whole social life, doctor, all those ladies and our little projects. And now I just sit at home in my armchair watching my daytime programs, feeling like a burden to everybody.
Do you feel any emotional pain or distress when these episodes happen, aside from feeling embarrassed or worried about what others think?

Well, emotional pain... I don't know if I'd call it pain, exactly. It's not like when I lost my husband, George, back in '98—now that was a heavy, aching kind of pain that just sat right on my chest for months. He had a bad heart, you know, and we always knew it was coming, but it still knocked the wind right out of me when it happened. 

But this? When my hand just keeps wiping that oatmeal bowl or when I'm stuck holding the broom up like a statue... it's more of a... a blankness, I suppose. I don't feel sad, or angry, or scared right in that moment. It's just like someone flipped a switch and turned the feelings off for a little bit. 

I mean, sure, afterward, when I snap out of it and realize I've been wiping the same spot on the counter for heaven knows how long, I get a little flustered. I think about what Mrs. Higgins next door would say if she looked through her kitchen window and saw me standing there like a fool. She's always been a bit of a gossip, that one. She told the whole neighborhood when the Miller boy backed his truck into the fire hydrant last summer, so I know she wouldn't keep quiet if she saw me acting strange. 

But during the actual... whatever you want to call it... the freezing up or the repeating things... no, there's no emotional distress at all. It's just quiet. My mind is just quiet, or maybe just humming along to a hymn, and my body is just doing its own peculiar thing. So, no, I wouldn't say it hurts my feelings or makes me upset while it's happening. It's just a strange, empty sort of feeling, if you can even call it a feeling at all.
Have you ever experienced episodes like these before, perhaps when you were younger?

When I was younger? Oh, my goodness, no. No, nothing like this ever happened to me back then. I was always sharp as a tack, quick on my feet. You had to be, with three younger brothers to look after while my mother was working at the textile mill. No, this... this freezing up and the repeating things, it's all very new. 

In fact, I can tell you exactly when it started. It's been going on for about eleven months now. Yes, eleven months. It all started right after my dearest friend, Martha, passed away. Martha Jenkins. We sang in the choir together for forty-two years. She was a soprano, had the voice of an absolute angel, could hit those high notes in "How Great Thou Art" without even straining her neck. We used to sit next to each other every Sunday, third row from the front, right side of the aisle. 

She got sick so suddenly... it was her pancreas, they said. She went into the hospital right around Thanksgiving, and by New Year's, she was gone. It was just terrible. We used to talk on the phone every single morning at 8:30, right after I finished my oatmeal and she finished her tea. We'd talk about the weather, or what the pastor said in his sermon, or how Mrs. Higgins' cat was digging up my petunias again. 

And after she died... well, that's when I started noticing these changes. I'd be standing in the kitchen, expecting the phone to ring at 8:30, and it wouldn't. And I'd just... get stuck. Just standing there with the dishcloth. Or I'd be at church, looking at her empty seat in the choir loft, and I'd get all confused about what we were supposed to be singing. So, no, doctor, it's not something from when I was young. It's just been these past eleven months, ever since I lost my Martha. It's like a piece of my routine just vanished, and my brain doesn't quite know how to fill in the gap, so it just... stops.
Have you experienced any other significant life changes or stressors in the past year, aside from the loss of your friend Martha?

Well, let me think on that for a minute... other changes... well, no, not really. I mean, my life is usually pretty quiet, just the way I like it. My son, David, he lives out in Ohio with his wife, Sarah, and their three girls. They're lovely girls, growing like weeds. The oldest, Emily, just started high school this year. Can you believe it? High school already. It feels like just yesterday she was running around my living room in her little pink tutu, knocking over my good lamp. Thankfully, it didn't break, just chipped the base a little, but I turned it toward the wall so nobody can see. 

But anyway, no, they haven't moved or anything. They've been in that same house in Cleveland for going on twelve years now. And my health, well, aside from these peculiar spells we've been talking about, my health has been pretty steady. Dr. Evans—he's my regular doctor, over at the clinic on Elm Street—he checks my blood pressure every six months, and he always says it's as good as a woman half my age. I take my little water pill every morning with my oatmeal, and that seems to keep everything ticking along just fine. 

I suppose the grocery store rearranged their aisles back in the spring, which was a terrible nuisance. I used to know exactly where the canned peaches were—aisle four, right next to the baking supplies—and they went and moved them all the way over to aisle seven by the breakfast cereals. I spent twenty minutes wandering around looking for them one Tuesday. But I wouldn't call that a major life stressor, just an annoyance, really. You know how they like to move things around just to confuse us older folks, make us walk past all the things we don't need so we'll buy them. 

So, no, doctor, besides losing my dear Martha, everything else has been just the same as it always is. Just my little house, my daytime programs, and trying to keep my garden looking nice, even though Mrs. Higgins' cat still thinks my petunias are his personal litter box. I've tried putting cayenne pepper in the dirt, I read that in a magazine at the hair salon, but that darn cat just sneezes and keeps right on digging. But no, no big changes or anything stressful like that. Just the usual day-to-day things.
Have you noticed any trouble remembering things that didn't used to be a problem for you?

Remembering things? Well... no, I can't say that I've had any trouble in that department. My memory is still as sharp as it ever was, thank the Lord. I mean, sure, if you ask me what I had for breakfast on a Tuesday three weeks ago, I might have to stop and think about it—though it was probably oatmeal, since I have my oatmeal every single morning at 7:45 right before I take my water pill. But no, real memory trouble? Not at all. 

I still know all the birthdays by heart without ever looking at a calendar. My son David is November 14th, and his girls... well, Emily is March 12th, and the twins, Chloe and Sophie, they were born on August 4th, right in the middle of that terrible heatwave. I send them a card every single year with a crisp five-dollar bill tucked inside. Never missed a year. And I still remember all my mother's recipes, too. Never wrote down her meatloaf recipe, but I know it takes exactly a half cup of breadcrumbs and a good pinch of sage. The sage is the secret, you see, it gives it a nice earthy flavor. 

And I don't even need a grocery list when I go to the store. I keep it all right up here in my head. I know I need a loaf of white bread, a half-gallon of 2% milk, and a tin of Folgers every Thursday. Even with them moving the aisles around like I told you, confusing everybody, I still know exactly what I went in there to get, even if I have to walk an extra mile to find it. 

Now, Mrs. Higgins next door, her memory is really going, though she’d never in a million years admit it. Just last week she asked me if I’d seen her gardening shears, and I had to remind her she left them sitting right on top of my rose bushes three days prior when she was leaning over the fence to complain about the mail carrier being late. But me? No. Aside from those peculiar spells where I just sort of get stuck or keep wiping the counter, my mind is perfectly clear. I remember the past, I remember what I need to do today, I remember all the verses to the hymns at church... so no, doctor, I haven't noticed any trouble with my memory whatsoever.
Have you ever seen, heard, or felt anything that wasn't really there?

Seen or heard things? Oh, my heavens, no. Like... like seeing ghosts or hearing voices, that sort of thing? Lord, no. I watch those mystery programs sometimes on the television—the ones on channel four right after the evening news, where they have those haunted houses and people claiming they hear things bumping in the night—and I always just shake my head and say, 'What a lot of nonsense.' I've never had anything peculiar like that happen to me, no sir. 

My eyes are still pretty good, you know. I mean, I do have to wear my little reading glasses for the Sunday paper and my word searches, but I can spot a dandelion in my front lawn from the kitchen window, clear across the yard. And my hearing is just fine, too. I can hear Mrs. Higgins' television through the wall sometimes when she has it turned up too loud. She loves that 'Wheel of Fortune' program, but she always guesses the wrong letters, bless her heart. I can hear her yelling out 'Z!' when it's clear as day a phrase that needs an 'E.' 

But hearing things that aren't there? Or seeing things? No, absolutely not. If I hear a noise in the house, I know it's just the floorboards settling, or the wind whistling through that old oak tree out back, or maybe that pesky cat knocking over my empty flower pots again. I've never imagined anything being there that wasn't. I'm very grounded, doctor. I just have those... those spells where I freeze up like we talked about, but my eyes and ears are working exactly the way they're supposed to.
Did you ever have any similar episodes or behaviors when you were under a lot of stress or going through a difficult time in your life before your friend Martha passed away?

Before Martha passed? Well, let me think back... you know, life is full of hard times, isn't it? It's not all sunshine and roses. But these spells, where I just get stuck or freeze up... no, I can't say I ever had anything like that happen before. I mean, I've been through my fair share of stress, don't get me wrong. 

When my husband, Arthur, passed away—oh, it's been nearly twenty-five years now—that was a terrible, terrible time. He had a heart attack right out in the driveway shoveling snow. It was a terrible storm, we got nearly two feet of snow overnight, and he was so stubborn, wouldn't wait for the neighbor boy to come do it. I told him, 'Arthur, leave it be, we aren't going anywhere anyway,' but you know how men are. He just had to get the driveway clear. Anyway, when he passed, I was heartbroken. I cried for weeks, couldn't hardly eat a thing except for some chicken broth Mrs. Higgins brought over. But I never froze up like this. I never just stopped in the middle of the kitchen staring at the wall, or got stuck wiping the exact same spot on the table for an hour. I was just sad, you know? Just regular, everyday grief. 

And then there was the time David moved all the way out to Ohio. That was awful hard on a mother. He packed up everything in this big yellow rental truck, and I remember standing on the porch waving goodbye, thinking my heart was just going to break right in two. I worried myself sick about him driving that giant truck on the highway, especially going through the mountains in Pennsylvania. I paced the floor all night long until he finally called from a motel in Toledo to say they made it that far safely. But even then, pacing the floor, I was moving. I wasn't stuck. 

So, no, doctor, these peculiar spells... they really just started up after my Martha went to be with the Lord. Before that, no matter how hard things got or how much I worried, I always kept moving right along, kept a clean house, kept my wits about me. It's just lately that my gears seem to get jammed up, so to speak. Never before this.
Do you feel like you're in control of your actions when these strange things happen, like holding the spoon or folding the napkins?

Control? Well, doctor, that's just the thing, and honestly, that is the whole entire reason I finally decided to come see you in the first place. I came because at church, I just keep doing these odd things, and I don't feel like I'm in charge of my own hands when it happens. 

We always have our fellowship hour right after the 10:30 Sunday service, down in the basement hall. Pastor Thomas says a lovely grace, and then we all line up for the potluck. But lately, I'll be standing right there by the potluck table, and I'll pick up the serving spoon—maybe for the macaroni salad, or Mary Alice's green bean casserole, she always puts those little crispy onions on top—and I'll just hold the serving spoon up in the air. And I just don't move. I stand there, completely frozen like a statue, holding that spoon up, and I can't seem to make my arm put it down into the bowl or scoop a single thing onto my paper plate. I just get stuck. 

Or, if I'm at the end of the table where the paper goods are, I'll start folding the napkins. I'll take a stack of those little square paper napkins, the cheap ones that tear if you even look at them wrong, and I'll just stand there folding the exact same stack over and over and over again. And the worst part is, the whole time, there is a whole line of people waiting on me! I know they're waiting, I can hear them shuffling their feet on the linoleum, and Mrs. Gable might clear her throat or sigh, but I just... I can't stop folding them, and I can't put the spoon down. 

It's not that I'm trying to be difficult or hold up the dinner line, doctor, I swear it. I just can't seem to make myself move on to the next thing. So no, I don't feel like I'm in control at all. It's terribly embarrassing, making a spectacle of myself like that while everyone's just wanting to get their supper. Like I said, that's exactly why I knew I had to come talk to you, because doing odd things like that in front of the whole congregation just isn't right.
Is there anything in particular that seems to trigger these episodes where you get stuck or repeat actions?

A trigger? You mean like... like something that sets it off? Well, doctor, I have racked my brain trying to figure that out myself. I really have. I'll sit in my recliner—the blue one by the front window, not the brown one, my Arthur bought that brown one in 1982 and the springs are completely shot, it just ruins my lower back—and I'll just sit there and think and think about it. But honestly? No. I can't say there's any rhyme or reason to it at all. 

Take last Tuesday, for example. It was a perfectly ordinary Tuesday. The weather was mild, just a lovely light breeze, not too humid like it gets in August. I had my toast with orange marmalade for breakfast, just exactly like I do every single morning, and I was feeling perfectly fine. I wasn't upset, I wasn't stressed about anything, my arthritis wasn't even acting up. I went into the sunroom to water my African violets—they're so finicky, you know, you can't get the leaves wet or they rot—and the next thing I know, I'm just standing there with my little green plastic watering can tipped over, frozen stiff as a board. The water just kept pouring out until the little clay saucer overflowed and made a terrible, muddy mess all over the linoleum. I ruined a perfectly good pair of house slippers, too, the water soaked right through to the fleece lining and you just can't wash those right without ruining the shape. 

So, you see, nothing caused it. Nobody had upset me, I wasn't thinking about my Martha, I wasn't worried about the electric bill or anything like that. It just... happens. Sometimes it's at church with the whole entire congregation waiting on me, and sometimes it's just me and my houseplants on a quiet morning. I wish I could tell you there was a pattern to it, like maybe it only happens when I'm tired or when I've had too much coffee, but I just haven't noticed anything of the sort. It just sneaks up on me, clear out of the blue, for no good reason that I can see.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep recently?

My sleep? Well, let me think on that... no, no, I wouldn't say there's been any changes at all in that department. I've always been a very good sleeper, doctor, ever since I was a little girl. My mother used to say a freight train could drive right through the parlor and I'd just sleep right on through the commotion. 

I have my routine, you see, and I stick to it religiously. I sit in the living room and watch the evening news—Channel 4, mind you, because I just cannot stand that new weatherman on Channel 7, he talks much too fast and he always gets the weekend forecast wrong anyway—and then right at 10 o'clock, I turn off the television set. I go around and check the locks on the front door and the back door, I make sure the burner on the stove is off, and I go right on up to bed. I have this wonderful heavy quilt, the one my sister Helen made for me back in 1998 for my birthday. It's a beautiful double-wedding-ring pattern with little blue and yellow flowers, all hand-stitched, and I just pull that right up under my chin. 

Once my head hits that pillow, I am out like a light. I sleep straight through the night until exactly 6:15 in the morning. I don't even need to set an alarm clock anymore, my body just knows. Sometimes that neighbor's dog, the big loud German Shepherd two houses down, will get to barking at a raccoon or a possum getting into the trash cans in the middle of the night, but even that doesn't stir me. I just sleep right on past it. So, no, my sleep is just exactly the same as it's always been. No trouble resting my eyes at all.
Have you ever lost consciousness or blacked out when these strange episodes happened?

Black out? Well... no. Oh, goodness no, doctor. Nothing like that at all. I am wide awake the entire time, clear as a bell. That's the part that makes it so terribly frustrating, you see. If I were blacking out or fainting—like my cousin Shirley used to do when she got overheated in the summertime, she'd just keel right over into the hydrangeas—well, then at least I wouldn't know what a spectacle I was making of myself! But no, I am completely conscious. 

When I get stuck holding that serving spoon over the macaroni salad, I can see every single thing happening around me. I can see the little red bits of pimento in the bowl, I can see Pastor Thomas talking to the choir director over by the refreshment table—he always drinks the red fruit punch, never the lemonade, says the acid gives him heartburn—and I can hear every little sound in that basement. I hear the fluorescent lights humming overhead, and I hear people shuffling their shoes, and I remember every single second of it. 

My mind is just as sharp as it's ever been, sitting right there inside my head, yelling at my arm to just put the spoon down, but my arm just won't listen. It's like I'm trapped inside myself. So no, I certainly don't lose consciousness. I am right there for every agonizing minute of it. Sometimes I tell you, I almost wish I *did* just pass out, because then people would just think I had a little dizzy spell or forgot to eat my breakfast, which is a perfectly respectable thing to happen to a woman my age. They'd just fetch me a glass of water and fan my face. But instead, I'm just standing there like a mannequin, wide awake, looking right back at everybody while they stare at me. So no, no blacking out. I remember it all, plain as day.
Do you feel any physical sensations, like tingling or numbness, right before you get stuck or start repeating actions?

Tingling? You mean like... like pins and needles? Well, now, let me think on that. I know exactly what you mean by numbness, of course. A few years back I was sitting on the floor with my granddaughter's little boy—he's just a rambunctious little thing, always wanting me to get down on the rug and play with those little wooden train sets of his—and I sat with my legs tucked under me for much too long. When I went to stand up, oh my stars, my whole left leg was completely dead to the world! It felt like a thousand little needles poking right into my heel when the blood finally started rushing back, and I had to hold onto the edge of the coffee table for a good five minutes before I could even take a step toward the kitchen. So I certainly know all about that feeling. 

But right before I get stuck like we were talking about? No... no, doctor, I can't say that I feel anything like that at all. Not a tingle, not a prickle, nothing. My body feels just as normal as it does right this very second sitting here talking to you. My hands feel perfectly fine, my arms feel fine, I don't get a chill or a hot flash or anything of the sort. 

That's the whole trouble with it, you see, there's just no warning whatsoever. If my fingers started to tingle, well, then I suppose I could at least put down whatever I'm holding before I freeze up! If I felt a little numbness coming on in my arm, I could set down my watering can, or I could put that serving spoon back in the macaroni salad bowl, and I wouldn't make such a terrible mess of things or make a spectacle of myself. I could just excuse myself and go sit down in a sturdy chair and wait for it to pass. But I don't get so much as a tap on the shoulder from my own body. I'm just moving along one second, feeling fit as a fiddle, and the next second, I'm stuck fast. So no, I don't feel any tingling or numbness at all before it happens.
Have you ever had recurring thoughts or urges that you felt compelled to act on, even before these episodes started happening?

Recurring thoughts? Urges? Well, now... let me just ponder on that for a minute. You mean like... like needing to wash my hands over and over, or checking the stove a dozen times? Oh, goodness, no. No, doctor, I've never had anything like that. I mean, I told you I check the locks and the stove before bed, but that's just once, you see. That's just good common sense. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, now she used to have to touch the doorknob exactly three times before she could leave her house. Three times, every single day! I used to watch her from my kitchen window while I was washing up the breakfast dishes. She'd step out onto her porch, grab the knob—one, two, three—and then she'd finally walk down the steps to get her mail. I always thought it was the most peculiar thing, but I never said a word to her about it, of course. It's not polite to pry into other people's habits. 

But for me? No, I've never felt compelled to do anything of the sort. My mind doesn't get stuck on thoughts like a broken record. I don't get these... these overwhelming urges to do things I don't want to do. I mean, aside from my arm getting stuck like we talked about, but that's entirely different, isn't it? That's not me *wanting* to do it or feeling an urge, that's just my body deciding to freeze up on me without asking my permission. 

Before all this started happening, my life was just as normal and quiet as could be. I'd wake up, I'd have my toast with a little bit of strawberry preserves—never the grape jelly, I find it much too sweet—and I'd go about my day, doing my gardening, maybe walking down to the market if I needed a few things. I never had any strange thoughts telling me to do things, and I certainly never had any urges I had to fight off. I just stay close to home, mostly. The most upsetting thing that happened to me all year—aside from poor Margaret, bless her heart—was when that big orange tomcat from three doors down got into my front flowerbeds and dug up half my spring bulbs. I had to go out there with my good sweeping broom and shoo him away, and then I spent a whole afternoon on my hands and knees replanting those bulbs, just praying they'd still come up in the spring. So, no. No accidents, no terrible frights, no other losses. I don't even watch the evening news anymore because all those awful stories they show just get my heart to racing for no good reason. It's just been a very plain, ordinary, quiet year... well, except for my body deciding to freeze up on me out of nowhere, of course. But other than that, no, nothing traumatic at all.

target_item.manifestation: Doctor, I came because at church I keep doing odd things, like standing by the potluck table holding the serving spoon up and not moving, or folding the same stack of napkins over and over while people are waiting on me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about my control over the odd behaviors I mentioned, such as holding the serving spoon and not moving, or folding the same napkins repeatedly, which relates directly to my disorganized and abnormal behavior.

patient.answer:
Control? Well, doctor, that's just the thing, and honestly, that is the whole entire reason I finally decided to come see you in the first place. I came because at church, I just keep doing these odd things, and I don't feel like I'm in charge of my own hands when it happens. 

We always have our fellowship hour right after the 10:30 Sunday service, down in the basement hall. Pastor Thomas says a lovely grace, and then we all line up for the potluck. But lately, I'll be standing right there by the potluck table, and I'll pick up the serving spoon—maybe for the macaroni salad, or Mary Alice's green bean casserole, she always puts those little crispy onions on top—and I'll just hold the serving spoon up in the air. And I just don't move. I stand there, completely frozen like a statue, holding that spoon up, and I can't seem to make my arm put it down into the bowl or scoop a single thing onto my paper plate. I just get stuck. 

Or, if I'm at the end of the table where the paper goods are, I'll start folding the napkins. I'll take a stack of those little square paper napkins, the cheap ones that tear if you even look at them wrong, and I'll just stand there folding the exact same stack over and over and over again. And the worst part is, the whole time, there is a whole line of people waiting on me! I know they're waiting, I can hear them shuffling their feet on the linoleum, and Mrs. Gable might clear her throat or sigh, but I just... I can't stop folding them, and I can't put the spoon down. 

It's not that I'm trying to be difficult or hold up the dinner line, doctor, I swear it. I just can't seem to make myself move on to the next thing. So no, I don't feel like I'm in control at all. It's terribly embarrassing, making a spectacle of myself like that while everyone's just wanting to get their supper. Like I said, that's exactly why I knew I had to come talk to you, because doing odd things like that in front of the whole congregation just isn't right.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences any triggers for the strange episodes
doctor.question: Is there anything in particular that seems to trigger these episodes where you get stuck or repeat actions?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about specific triggers for the disorganized/abnormal behavior, which is not covered in the symptom profile.

patient.answer:
A trigger? You mean like... like something that sets it off? Well, doctor, I have racked my brain trying to figure that out myself. I really have. I'll sit in my recliner—the blue one by the front window, not the brown one, my Arthur bought that brown one in 1982 and the springs are completely shot, it just ruins my lower back—and I'll just sit there and think and think about it. But honestly? No. I can't say there's any rhyme or reason to it at all. 

Take last Tuesday, for example. It was a perfectly ordinary Tuesday. The weather was mild, just a lovely light breeze, not too humid like it gets in August. I had my toast with orange marmalade for breakfast, just exactly like I do every single morning, and I was feeling perfectly fine. I wasn't upset, I wasn't stressed about anything, my arthritis wasn't even acting up. I went into the sunroom to water my African violets—they're so finicky, you know, you can't get the leaves wet or they rot—and the next thing I know, I'm just standing there with my little green plastic watering can tipped over, frozen stiff as a board. The water just kept pouring out until the little clay saucer overflowed and made a terrible, muddy mess all over the linoleum. I ruined a perfectly good pair of house slippers, too, the water soaked right through to the fleece lining and you just can't wash those right without ruining the shape. 

So, you see, nothing caused it. Nobody had upset me, I wasn't thinking about my Martha, I wasn't worried about the electric bill or anything like that. It just... happens. Sometimes it's at church with the whole entire congregation waiting on me, and sometimes it's just me and my houseplants on a quiet morning. I wish I could tell you there was a pattern to it, like maybe it only happens when I'm tired or when I've had too much coffee, but I just haven't noticed anything of the sort. It just sneaks up on me, clear out of the blue, for no good reason that I can see.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any significant changes in their sleep patterns
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your sleep recently?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in sleep, which is not covered by any of the provided symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
My sleep? Well, let me think on that... no, no, I wouldn't say there's been any changes at all in that department. I've always been a very good sleeper, doctor, ever since I was a little girl. My mother used to say a freight train could drive right through the parlor and I'd just sleep right on through the commotion. 

I have my routine, you see, and I stick to it religiously. I sit in the living room and watch the evening news—Channel 4, mind you, because I just cannot stand that new weatherman on Channel 7, he talks much too fast and he always gets the weekend forecast wrong anyway—and then right at 10 o'clock, I turn off the television set. I go around and check the locks on the front door and the back door, I make sure the burner on the stove is off, and I go right on up to bed. I have this wonderful heavy quilt, the one my sister Helen made for me back in 1998 for my birthday. It's a beautiful double-wedding-ring pattern with little blue and yellow flowers, all hand-stitched, and I just pull that right up under my chin. 

Once my head hits that pillow, I am out like a light. I sleep straight through the night until exactly 6:15 in the morning. I don't even need to set an alarm clock anymore, my body just knows. Sometimes that neighbor's dog, the big loud German Shepherd two houses down, will get to barking at a raccoon or a possum getting into the trash cans in the middle of the night, but even that doesn't stir me. I just sleep right on past it. So, no, my sleep is just exactly the same as it's always been. No trouble resting my eyes at all.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any loss of consciousness during the episodes
doctor.question: Have you ever lost consciousness or blacked out when these strange episodes happened?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about loss of consciousness or blacking out, which is not covered by any of my symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Black out? Well... no. Oh, goodness no, doctor. Nothing like that at all. I am wide awake the entire time, clear as a bell. That's the part that makes it so terribly frustrating, you see. If I were blacking out or fainting—like my cousin Shirley used to do when she got overheated in the summertime, she'd just keel right over into the hydrangeas—well, then at least I wouldn't know what a spectacle I was making of myself! But no, I am completely conscious. 

When I get stuck holding that serving spoon over the macaroni salad, I can see every single thing happening around me. I can see the little red bits of pimento in the bowl, I can see Pastor Thomas talking to the choir director over by the refreshment table—he always drinks the red fruit punch, never the lemonade, says the acid gives him heartburn—and I can hear every little sound in that basement. I hear the fluorescent lights humming overhead, and I hear people shuffling their shoes, and I remember every single second of it. 

My mind is just as sharp as it's ever been, sitting right there inside my head, yelling at my arm to just put the spoon down, but my arm just won't listen. It's like I'm trapped inside myself. So no, I certainly don't lose consciousness. I am right there for every agonizing minute of it. Sometimes I tell you, I almost wish I *did* just pass out, because then people would just think I had a little dizzy spell or forgot to eat my breakfast, which is a perfectly respectable thing to happen to a woman my age. They'd just fetch me a glass of water and fan my face. But instead, I'm just standing there like a mannequin, wide awake, looking right back at everybody while they stare at me. So no, no blacking out. I remember it all, plain as day.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences any physical sensations before the episodes
doctor.question: Do you feel any physical sensations, like tingling or numbness, right before you get stuck or start repeating actions?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about physical sensations like tingling or numbness preceding the episodes, which is not covered by my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Tingling? You mean like... like pins and needles? Well, now, let me think on that. I know exactly what you mean by numbness, of course. A few years back I was sitting on the floor with my granddaughter's little boy—he's just a rambunctious little thing, always wanting me to get down on the rug and play with those little wooden train sets of his—and I sat with my legs tucked under me for much too long. When I went to stand up, oh my stars, my whole left leg was completely dead to the world! It felt like a thousand little needles poking right into my heel when the blood finally started rushing back, and I had to hold onto the edge of the coffee table for a good five minutes before I could even take a step toward the kitchen. So I certainly know all about that feeling. 

But right before I get stuck like we were talking about? No... no, doctor, I can't say that I feel anything like that at all. Not a tingle, not a prickle, nothing. My body feels just as normal as it does right this very second sitting here talking to you. My hands feel perfectly fine, my arms feel fine, I don't get a chill or a hot flash or anything of the sort. 

That's the whole trouble with it, you see, there's just no warning whatsoever. If my fingers started to tingle, well, then I suppose I could at least put down whatever I'm holding before I freeze up! If I felt a little numbness coming on in my arm, I could set down my watering can, or I could put that serving spoon back in the macaroni salad bowl, and I wouldn't make such a terrible mess of things or make a spectacle of myself. I could just excuse myself and go sit down in a sturdy chair and wait for it to pass. But I don't get so much as a tap on the shoulder from my own body. I'm just moving along one second, feeling fit as a fiddle, and the next second, I'm stuck fast. So no, I don't feel any tingling or numbness at all before it happens.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has a history of obsessive-compulsive behavior
doctor.question: Have you ever had recurring thoughts or urges that you felt compelled to act on, even before these episodes started happening?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about obsessive-compulsive symptoms (recurring thoughts or urges), which are not covered in the provided symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Recurring thoughts? Urges? Well, now... let me just ponder on that for a minute. You mean like... like needing to wash my hands over and over, or checking the stove a dozen times? Oh, goodness, no. No, doctor, I've never had anything like that. I mean, I told you I check the locks and the stove before bed, but that's just once, you see. That's just good common sense. My neighbor, Mrs. Gable, now she used to have to touch the doorknob exactly three times before she could leave her house. Three times, every single day! I used to watch her from my kitchen window while I was washing up the breakfast dishes. She'd step out onto her porch, grab the knob—one, two, three—and then she'd finally walk down the steps to get her mail. I always thought it was the most peculiar thing, but I never said a word to her about it, of course. It's not polite to pry into other people's habits. 

But for me? No, I've never felt compelled to do anything of the sort. My mind doesn't get stuck on thoughts like a broken record. I don't get these... these overwhelming urges to do things I don't want to do. I mean, aside from my arm getting stuck like we talked about, but that's entirely different, isn't it? That's not me *wanting* to do it or feeling an urge, that's just my body deciding to freeze up on me without asking my permission. 

Before all this started happening, my life was just as normal and quiet as could be. I'd wake up, I'd have my toast with a little bit of strawberry preserves—never the grape jelly, I find it much too sweet—and I'd go about my day, doing my gardening, maybe walking down to the market if I needed a few things. I never had any strange thoughts telling me to do things, and I certainly never had any urges I had to fight off. My mind has always been my own, doctor, and it's always been a very sensible, quiet sort of mind. So no, nothing like that at all. Just a regular life, right up until my body decided to start playing these terrible tricks on me.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences any obsessive thoughts or compulsions outside of the freezing episodes
doctor.question: Do you have any thoughts that keep repeating in your mind, even when you're not having one of these freezing episodes?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about recurring or repeating thoughts (obsessions), which is not covered by the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Repeating thoughts? Well... no, doctor, I really don't. I know we just talked about urges and such a moment ago, and it's much the same for just plain thoughts. My mind doesn't get stuck on a loop, if that's what you're asking. 

Now, I know some folks who just can't let a thought go, I certainly do. My late husband, George, God rest his soul, if he thought the carburetor on the Buick was making a funny noise, he would talk about it all through supper, all through the evening news, and right up until we turned the bedside lamp off. Just over and over, 'I think it's the carburetor, Martha, I really do.' And I'd say, 'Well then take it down to the mechanic tomorrow, George!' But he'd just keep chewing on that same thought like a dog with an old slipper. He couldn't help himself, his mind just worked that way, always worrying a problem down to the bone.

But me? I've never been that way at all. My mind is very... well, it's just very ordinary and quiet. When I'm not having one of those awful freezing spells, I'm just living my regular life. I'll sit in my armchair in the afternoon—I have a lovely floral armchair right by the front window so I can watch the street and see who's coming and going—and I might think about what I'm going to make for supper. I might think, 'Oh, a nice piece of baked chicken would be good today, maybe with some boiled carrots and a pinch of dill.' And then that thought is done, you see? I don't keep thinking about the chicken. I move right along to thinking about how the rhododendrons need pruning, or wondering if the mailman has come by yet. 

Nothing just spins around and around in my head. It's peaceful up there. Well, peaceful until my body decides to turn me into a statue, of course! But the thoughts themselves? No, they don't repeat at all. They just come and go, plain and simple, like clouds passing by the window.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any significant changes in their appetite or eating habits
doctor.question: Have you noticed any changes in your appetite or eating habits recently?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about changes in appetite or eating habits, which is not covered by any of the symptom profiles.

patient.answer:
Changes in my eating? Well, now... let me think on that. No, I can't say that I have. My appetite is just exactly the same as it's always been, regular as a clock. 

I've always been a very steady eater, you see. Three square meals a day, just like my mother taught us when we were coming up. Like I mentioned a moment ago about my morning toast and strawberry preserves—I still have that every single morning at seven o'clock sharp, along with a nice cup of weak black tea. Sometimes I'll have half a grapefruit if they look decent down at the market, but only if they're on sale, because the prices they're asking for fruit these days, well, it's just highway robbery, I tell you. 

And then for lunch, I keep it very simple. I might make myself a little egg salad sandwich on wheat bread, or heat up a bowl of tomato soup if there's a bit of a chill in the air. I always eat every last bite. I certainly haven't lost my taste for things. Just yesterday evening, I made myself a lovely little meatloaf for supper. Just a small one, of course, since it's only me in the house now, but I put a pinch of dry mustard in the meat mixture—that's a little trick my sister Eleanor taught me years and years ago, it gives it such a wonderful savory flavor without being too spicy. I had a good thick slice of that, along with some mashed potatoes and a handful of green beans, and I enjoyed every bit of it. 

So no, doctor, my stomach is doing just fine. I get hungry right when I'm supposed to, right around noon for lunch and five-thirty for supper, and I eat my regular portions just like I always have. I haven't been skipping meals, and I haven't been eating the house down, either. Everything in the kitchen department is just as normal as can be.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has experienced any traumatic events recently
doctor.question: Have you experienced any traumatic events in the last year, aside from the loss of your friend Martha?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about other traumatic events, which is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Traumatic events? Well, now... first of all, doctor, *I* am Martha! I think you might have your notes just a little bit mixed up there. Like I said before, George always called me Martha, because that's my name! You must be thinking of my dear friend Margaret who passed away last November. Or... wait, was it October? No, it had to be November, because I remember clear as day I had to wear my heavy wool coat to the funeral, the navy blue one with the big tortoise-shell buttons that I bought down at the old department store years and years ago. But yes, losing Margaret was a terrible, terrible blow. We used to sit on my porch and shell peas together in the summer, and she was the only one who knew how to make a proper angel food cake from scratch. 

But aside from losing her? No, goodness no. I haven't had any other... traumatic events, as you call them. My life is very quiet, very sheltered, I suppose you could say. I don't go out looking for trouble, and thankfully, trouble doesn't usually come looking for me. 

I just stay close to home, mostly. The most upsetting thing that happened to me all year—aside from poor Margaret, bless her heart—was when that big orange tomcat from three doors down got into my front flowerbeds and dug up half my spring bulbs. Oh, I was so mad I could have spit! I had to go out there with my good sweeping broom and shoo him away, and then I spent a whole afternoon on my hands and knees replanting those bulbs, just praying they'd still come up in the spring. And they did, mostly, though the daffodils were a little sparse. But you can't really call a cat in the tulips a trauma, can you? 

So, no. No accidents, no terrible frights, no other losses. I don't even watch the evening news anymore because all those awful stories they show just get my heart to racing for no good reason. It's just been a very plain, ordinary, quiet year... well, except for my body deciding to freeze up on me out of nowhere, of course. But other than that, no, nothing traumatic at all.
